**Regulatory Strategy Memo: AI Pneumothorax Flagging on Chest X-Ray (US and EU)**

*Provisional analysis, for confirmation by RA, your notified body, and FDA. As of 23 October 2026; re-verify each source (FDA guidance database, eCFR, EUR-Lex, MDCG page) before relying on it.*

### 1. Bottom line
- **US:** A device software function. It analyzes a medical image, so it fails criterion 1 of the section 520(o)(1)(E) CDS exclusion, and explainability doesn't change that. Likely route: **510(k)**, since cleared chest X-ray pneumothorax triage devices exist.
- **EU:** Medical device software (MDR Art. 2(1), MDCG 2019-11). Rule 11 makes it IIa at minimum; **plan for IIb**. Contract a notified body now, because their capacity may set your EU launch date.
- **The decision that drives both:** triage (worklist notification only, image untouched) or detection (marks the finding on the image)? Different regulation, different evidence.

### 2. Draft intended use (triage version)
> [Product] is software intended to analyze frontal chest X-rays of adults and notify radiologists of cases with suspected pneumothorax to prioritize their review. It does not mark or alter the original image, remove cases from the worklist, or provide a diagnosis. Radiologists review all images per standard of care.

**Claims audit:** "detects pneumothorax," "reduces missed findings," "faster chest drains," "replaces the second read," or use by ED physicians would each exceed this intended use. FDA (21 CFR 801.4) and MDR Art. 2(12) read your website, deck, and sales scripts, not just the IFU.

### 3. US pathway
| Option | Regulation | Class | Typical evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Triage | 21 CFR 892.2080, radiological computer-aided triage and notification software | II, special controls | Standalone performance, time-to-notification |
| Detection with localization | 21 CFR 892.2070, medical image analyzer (CADe) | II | Standalone plus multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) study |

Autonomous or rule-out claims fit neither and push you toward De Novo or beyond. Verify the regulation and product code in FDA's product classification database.

- **Predicate:** same intended use, from FDA's 510(k) database and AI-enabled device list. No split predicates.
- **Submission:** eSTAR. Software documentation per FDA's 2023 device software functions guidance. Basic level is plausible for triage, since a missed flag leaves the case in normal reading order, but the guidance assesses risk *before* risk controls, so let your risk analysis decide. PACS connectivity likely makes it a **cyber device (section 524B)**: threat model, SBOM, vulnerability management plan.
- **PCCP** per FDA's December 2024 final guidance: retraining, new X-ray manufacturers, operating-point changes, each with a modification protocol. Changes outside it go through FDA's software-change assessment and may need a new 510(k).
- **QMS:** QMSR (effective 2 February 2026) incorporates ISO 13485:2016, so one QMS serves both markets.

### 4. EU pathway
- **Class:** information used for diagnostic decisions means IIa at minimum. A missed tension pneumothorax can cause serious deterioration, and treatment is a chest drain (arguably a surgical intervention), so **IIb is my planning assumption**. Ask the notified body early.
- **Route:** notified body assessment of QMS and technical documentation; clinical evaluation per Art. 61 and MDCG 2020-1 (valid clinical association, technical and clinical performance); PMS, PMCF, PSUR; a PRRC (Art. 15); an authorised representative if you're outside the EU; UDI and EUDAMED; cybersecurity per Annex I §17 and MDCG 2019-16.
- **Model changes:** MDR has no PCCP equivalent. Agree in writing with the notified body which changes need prior approval.
- **EU AI Act:** high-risk (Art. 6(1), Annex I). The application date for device AI (originally 2 August 2027) has faced proposed postponement; verify on EUR-Lex. Build one technical file for both regimes.

### 5. One evidence plan, both markets
- Retrospective standalone study on data from sites and X-ray manufacturers **not used in training**; AP and PA, portable and fixed
- Reference standard: blinded radiologist consensus, CT where available
- Sensitivity, specificity, and AUC with 95% CIs against pre-specified acceptance criteria; time-to-notification for triage
- Subgroups: sex, age, site, manufacturer, projection, pneumothorax size, and **chest drain present** (models can learn the drain instead of the pneumothorax)
- A statistician sizes it; the EU clinical evaluation reuses it

### 6. Quality system and lifecycle
- IEC 62304: provisionally **class B**, relying on radiologist review as an external risk control. Document the rationale; if you can't justify it, it's C.
- One ISO 14971 risk file covering missed pneumothorax, wrong-patient results, poor images analyzed silently, alert fatigue, and automation bias, linked to IEC 62366-1 usability and security threats.
- SOUP, cloud services, and any third-party model: versioned, monitored, and in the SBOM.
- State in writing where design controls start, and lock the model version you'll submit.

### 7. Sequence (planning assumptions; replace with real quotes)
1. Weeks 0–4: intended use, claims audit, determination memo per market, triage-vs-CADe decision.
2. Now: notified body shortlist and contract.
3. Pre-Sub (allow about 70–75 days to feedback): predicate and indications, standalone study protocol, PCCP scope.
4. QMS, design controls, V&V, standalone study.
5. 510(k): 90 FDA review days, with the clock stopped during holds. EU notified body review often takes a year or more.

US first is typical given available predicates; build the EU file in parallel from one core technical documentation.

### 8. What I need from you
Triage or localization? Radiologists only? Adults only, and which X-ray vendors? Any third-party foundation model?

**IEC 62304 Software Development Plan: Outline for Class B SaMD**

*As of 23 October 2026, based on IEC 62304:2006+A1:2015. A new edition has been in development, so confirm which edition FDA recognizes and your notified body expects before you baseline. Clause applicability is my summary of Table A.1; check it against the standard.*

Keep it lean: reference your SOPs instead of repeating them, and name an owner for every activity.

### 0. Document control and documentation planning (5.1.2, 5.1.8)
ID, version, owner, approvers, revision history. List every planned document with its ID, author, reviewer, approver, and storage location. Update the plan as you go; auditors compare it with what you actually did.

### 1. Scope and references
- Software system, items, and deployment (cloud, mobile, on-premise) in scope
- Link to ISO 13485 §7.3 design and development planning and your design control SOP
- Related standards: ISO 14971, IEC 62366-1, IEC 81001-5-1 (security), and IEC 82304-1 (product-level requirements and validation, which 62304 doesn't cover)

### 2. Safety classification (4.3)
- Class B rationale: the hazardous situations the software can contribute to, and why the worst credible harm is non-serious injury once risk controls *external* to the software are considered. Cite the risk file.
- Reclassification triggers; any items segregated at a different class
- FDA documentation level (Basic or Enhanced), recorded separately because it is a different determination

### 3. Lifecycle, deliverables, and roles (5.1.1, 5.1.3)
- Lifecycle model; for agile, map sprints to 62304 activities (AAMI TIR45 helps) and put the required records in your definition of done
- Deliverables table: activity, output, owner, reviewer, milestone
- How system requirements feed software requirements, and how system V&V uses software outputs

### 4. Software requirements (5.2)
Functional, performance, interface, alarm and warning, security, data, usability-derived, and labeling requirements, plus every risk control implemented in software. Re-evaluate the risk analysis when requirements change.

### 5. Architecture and units (5.3, 5.4.1)
Software items and interfaces; functional and performance requirements for each SOUP item and the platform it needs; segregation where a risk control depends on it; architecture verification. Subdivide into software units (no unit-level detailed design required at class B).

### 6. Implementation and unit verification (5.5)
Coding standards, code review, static analysis, unit tests, and unit acceptance criteria. Say where the records live (pull request approvals, CI logs).

### 7. Integration, system testing, and verification planning (5.1.5, 5.1.6, 5.6, 5.7)
Integration sequence and environment; system test protocols traced to every requirement and risk control; pass/fail criteria; regression rules after changes; anomaly evaluation; who verifies what, at which milestone.

### 8. Software risk management (5.1.7, 7)
Reference the ISO 14971 plan. Identify software items contributing to hazardous situations and their causes, including SOUP failure and security threats. Implement controls as requirements, verify them, and analyze the risk of every change.

### 9. Configuration management (5.1.9–5.1.11, 8)
- Configuration items: source, build scripts, documents, SOUP, and for AI, models and datasets
- SOUP list: name, supplier, version, purpose, anomaly monitoring
- Supporting items under control (compilers, CI, test tools) and items under control before verification
- Branching, baselines, change control, reproducible builds

### 10. Problem resolution (9)
Problem report content, investigation, safety impact, trend review, and links to CAPA and complaint handling.

### 11. Common software defects (5.1.12)
Name the defect categories relevant to your stack (CWE Top 25, for example) and how standards, static analysis, and tests prevent them. Auditors often find this section empty.

### 12. Release (5.8)
Verification complete, residual anomalies evaluated and listed, version identified, build environment documented, release archived, delivery reliable.

### 13. Maintenance (6)
Feedback intake, modification analysis, and a documented regulatory change assessment for every release (FDA's software-change 510(k) guidance; your notified body's change procedure).

### 14. Tools and standards (5.1.4)
Required only at class C, but cheap to include. Validate tools that hold quality records (ISO 13485 §4.1.6, incorporated into FDA's QMSR since 2 February 2026).

### 15. Addenda, if applicable
Security: threat model, SBOM, vulnerability handling. AI: data management, train/test separation, model versioning, and your change plan (PCCP in the US).

### Class B vs class C
You skip detailed unit design (5.4.2–5.4.4), additional unit acceptance criteria (5.5.4), and tools planning (5.1.4). You don't skip architecture, unit verification, integration testing, or the full risk, configuration, and problem-resolution processes.

**Gaps I see most often:** a class B rationale that never names its external risk controls, SOUP listed without versions or requirements, and releases that ship with an unverified risk control. Gate every release on a traceability check.

Send me your hazard analysis and I'll check that class B holds before you build the plan around it.
